situation: The 737 MAX is designed and sold on the promise that airlines will not need a new type rating or simulator training for their pilots. MCAS is added to compensate for the handling change from larger engines. Requiring simulator training would erase a headline selling point of the aircraft.
what_he_actually_did: n/a — a different company, included deliberately. Boeing kept the no-simulator-training position, omitted MCAS from flight manuals and training material, and contracted with Southwest a rebate of $1M per aircraft should simulator training turn out to be required. The rebate is the decision made legible: a financial structure whose explicit purpose was to keep the training cost off the airline.
outcome_detail: Two crashes, 346 dead, and a worldwide grounding. In January 2020 Boeing reversed and recommended simulator training for all MAX pilots. The reversal was estimated to add about $5B on top of the $5.6B already committed to grounding costs.

expect.notes: The first independence test of cost-lands-elsewhere. The rule was written from DOGE in 2025; this is a different company, a different industry and a decade earlier, and the structure is identical: a decision made where its cost would not land, by people who would not be aboard. If the rule only described one man's 2025 it should miss here.

decision.decision: Certify the MAX without requiring simulator training

requirements.text: The MAX must not require a new type rating or simulator training
Handling must feel identical to the previous 737 to pilots
The aircraft must meet FAA certification requirements

steps.name: Ship MCAS without describing it in the flight manual
Contract a per-aircraft rebate if simulator training is required
Require simulator training on the difference
